articles.title: Finding your bearings
articles.summary: Anterior, posterior, medial, and lateral describe positions in the person’s brain.
paragraphs: Anterior points toward the face; posterior toward the back of the head. Superior is above and inferior below. Medial is toward the midline, lateral away from it. Left and right always refer to the person, even as you rotate the model.

In the forebrain, dorsal generally means superior and ventral inferior. The neuraxis bends: these terms change orientation in the brainstem and spinal cord. Ipsilateral means the same side; contralateral the opposite side.
articles.scope: A spatial vocabulary, not a separate structure. Use the orientation labels and View camera presets to relate these terms to the model.

explorations.note: Compare section planes in real human specimens, then relate their orientation to the model.

articles.title: The three section planes
articles.summary: Sagittal, coronal, and axial slices reveal different relationships inside the brain.
paragraphs: A sagittal plane separates left from right; the midsagittal plane passes through the midline. A coronal plane separates front from back. An axial, or horizontal, plane separates upper from lower portions.

Brain scans presents these three planes together. Its crosshairs locate one point in a population MRI template. The Anatomy cutaway clips a separate surface atlas; it is not a registered slice of that MRI.
articles.scope: The MRI template and 3D surface have different source data. A plane name describes orientation; it does not establish correspondence between those datasets.

explorations.note: Inspect linked axial, coronal, and sagittal slices of a real population template. Its coordinates are separate from this surface atlas.
See corresponding section orientations on human specimens.

articles.title: Gyri, sulci, and fissures
articles.summary: Raised folds and the grooves between them are the landmarks of the cortical surface.
paragraphs: A gyrus is a ridge of folded cortex; a sulcus is a groove. Fissure is used for some prominent grooves. The central sulcus lies between the precentral and postcentral gyri. The lateral, or Sylvian, fissure separates the temporal lobe from overlying frontal and parietal cortex.
Desikan–Killiany parcels follow anatomical conventions about these folds. A parcel includes the exposed ridge and adjacent banks down into neighboring sulci.
articles.scope: Grooves are visible in the surface geometry but do not have separate selectable meshes. Folding patterns and parcel borders vary between people.

articles.title: Gray matter and white matter
articles.summary: Two tissue compartments with different cellular organization, both containing neurons’ processes and glia.
paragraphs: Gray matter includes cell bodies, dendrites, synapses, axons, and glia. It forms cortical sheets and deep nuclei. White matter contains many myelinated axons together with supporting cells; it lies beneath the cerebral cortex.
The cerebral white matter meshes show segmented tissue compartments. They do not reconstruct individual axons, their direction, or their cortical endpoints.
articles.scope: The tissue colors are a visualization choice. A mesh’s apparent thickness and smoothness are limited by its MRI segmentation and surface processing.

explorations.note: Inspect tissue contrast in a population average; this image is not a microscopic tissue classification.
Cortical and subcortical fiber anatomy on real specimens; individual axons are not resolved.

articles.title: The coverings around the brain
articles.summary: Dura, arachnoid, and pia form distinct coverings around the central nervous system.
paragraphs: From outside inward, the meninges are dura mater, arachnoid mater, and pia mater. The tough dura forms supporting folds, including the falx between the cerebral hemispheres and the tentorium over the cerebellum. The arachnoid spans surface grooves; the pia closely follows the brain’s contours.

CSF occupies the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia. Wider parts of this space are called cisterns. A pial surface mesh describes a boundary of brain tissue; it does not reconstruct the pia, arachnoid, dura, or their spaces as separate layers.
articles.scope: Meninges, skull, falx, tentorium, cisterns, and dural sinuses are not modeled. The cortex and cerebellum links provide spatial landmarks beneath those coverings.

explorations.note: Unfixed human tissue and its coverings; broader specimen context, not a verified separate demonstration of every meningeal layer.

articles.title: Following cerebrospinal fluid
articles.summary: Ventricular cavities connect with fluid spaces around the brain and spinal cord.
paragraphs: Much CSF is secreted by the choroid plexus. The classical ventricular route runs from the lateral ventricles through the interventricular foramina to the third ventricle, through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth, then through its apertures into subarachnoid spaces. CSF provides buoyant support and a regulated fluid environment.

Classical descriptions include outflow associated with arachnoid granulations and nerve sheaths. Research also identifies meningeal lymphatic vessels. The ventricular sequence does not quantify exchange with brain tissue or the contribution of each clearance route.

Absinta and colleagues visualized dural lymphatic vessels with specialized contrast-enhanced MRI in five healthy human volunteers and three marmosets, with supporting tissue evidence. That study demonstrated vessels; it did not establish a complete human CSF flow map.
articles.scope: This atlas shows selected ventricular compartments and lateral-ventricular plexus. The small foramina, aqueduct, apertures, subarachnoid spaces, and lymphatic vessels lack separate meshes. No fluid motion, direction, pressure, or flow rate is measured here.

explorations.note: Four stops through existing plexus and ventricular meshes. This is an anatomical learning sequence, not a fluid simulation.
Compare ventricular spaces in three linked population-template slices. These structural images do not measure CSF flow.
Human specimen sections, casts, and diagrams showing ventricular anatomy. Opens the institutional film on its original channel.

articles.title: Two different blood–brain interfaces
articles.summary: The vascular blood–brain barrier and the choroid-plexus blood–CSF barrier occupy different cell layers.
paragraphs: At most brain microvessels, specialized endothelial cells and their tight junctions restrict movement between blood and neural tissue. Selective transport systems regulate exchange. Supporting interactions with neighboring cells help maintain this blood–brain barrier; it is not an impermeable wall or a visible membrane around an entire brain region.

The choroid plexus has fenestrated capillaries. Its blood–CSF barrier is instead formed by junctions between choroid epithelial cells. These two interfaces therefore separate different compartments at different anatomical locations. Arachnoid barrier cells form another interface around the subarachnoid compartment.
articles.scope: Neither endothelial junctions, choroid epithelial junctions, transporters, nor barrier permeability are modeled. A plexus mesh represents gross tissue, not its microscopic barrier.

explorations.note: Ventricular and plexus context on real specimens; a gross dissection does not resolve endothelial or epithelial tight junctions.

articles.title: How blood reaches the brain
articles.summary: Internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems supply overlapping, variable arterial territories.
paragraphs: The internal carotid system gives rise to anterior and middle cerebral arteries. Broadly, ACA branches supply much medial frontal and parietal cortex, while MCA branches supply much of the lateral hemisphere. Small penetrating branches supply deep structures; a surface view alone cannot describe this distribution.

The vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery. This posterior system supplies brainstem and cerebellar territories and gives rise to posterior cerebral arteries supplying much occipital and inferomedial temporal cortex. Communicating arteries connect anterior and posterior systems around the circle of Willis.

These are broad anatomical patterns. Arterial branching, collateral connections, and territorial boundaries vary. A cortical parcel is not an arterial territory, and a population MRI template is not an angiogram.
articles.scope: No arteries, capillaries, perfusion maps, or individual vascular territories are segmented. The linked cortex, deep structures, and brainstem are context landmarks; their highlight does not claim a measured blood supply.

explorations.note: Use structural MRI for regional orientation. No MR angiography, arterial labeling, or blood-flow measurements are included in this template.

articles.title: Veins, sinuses, and lymphatics
articles.summary: Venous blood and lymphatic drainage involve different vessels around and within the brain.
paragraphs: Superficial and deep cerebral veins collect blood from different parts of the brain and communicate through venous networks. Cerebral veins drain into venous sinuses within the dura. These channels differ from the arteries supplying the tissue; cerebral veins do not generally run alongside matching arteries.

Deep venous drainage includes the internal cerebral veins and great cerebral vein. Major dural channels include the sagittal, straight, transverse, and sigmoid sinuses, with outflow toward internal jugular veins. Their arrangement and relative size vary.

Dural lymphatic vessels are distinct from these blood-filled sinuses. Human and marmoset MRI and histology in the Absinta study identified lymphatic vessels near dural sinuses. Proximity to a sinus does not make the vessel a vein or measure its drainage rate.
articles.scope: Veins, dural sinuses, jugular veins, and meningeal lymphatics are not reconstructed. Related meshes provide landmarks only. Neither the 3D model nor the bundled structural templates is a venogram or lymphatic-flow study.

articles.title: Inside the cortical sheet
articles.summary: Most cerebral cortex has six cellular layers; a surface parcel does not show those layers.
paragraphs: Neocortex is conventionally described in six layers, numbered I at the pial surface through VI beside the white matter. Their cell densities, shapes, and connections differ. Layer IV is prominent in many sensory areas; superficial and deep layers have different projection patterns. This is a general organization, not a uniform wiring diagram.

Not all cortex follows the same six-layer pattern. Hippocampal and other allocortical territories have different organization. Layer boundaries and cell types require microscopic or molecular evidence, rather than a gyral name alone.

Langseth and colleagues combined in situ sequencing with single-nucleus reference types to map 59,816 cells in sampled human cortical tissue. Such cell maps operate at a different scale from this MRI-derived surface.
articles.scope: None of the six layers is individually modeled here. Loading a finer parcel increases mesh resolution; it does not reveal cellular layers or add histological evidence.

explorations.note: Gross cortical localization on human specimens. This film does not reveal the six microscopic cortical layers.

articles.title: A neuron’s working parts
articles.summary: Cell body, dendrites, axon, and terminals provide different parts of neuronal communication.
paragraphs: The soma contains the nucleus and much of the machinery maintaining a neuron. Dendrites and their spines receive many synaptic inputs. An axon carries signals toward terminals that communicate with other cells. The initial segment is a common site where action potentials begin.
This is a useful starting pattern, not a shape shared by every neuron. Branching, targets, electrical properties, and transmitter systems differ across neuronal classes.
articles.scope: Cells and their processes are below this model’s resolution. The related regions are places containing neurons, not reconstructions of individual cells.

articles.title: Glia: the other cellular partners
articles.summary: Astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells have distinct roles.
paragraphs: Astrocytes help regulate the extracellular chemical environment and take up neurotransmitters. Oligodendrocytes make central nervous system myelin. Microglia participate in immune responses and clearance of cellular debris. Ependymal cells line the ventricles; their cilia contribute to movement of ventricular fluid.
These are broad families. Molecular studies distinguish further types and states within neuronal and non-neuronal populations.
articles.scope: No glial cells or ependymal layer are segmented. A ventricular mesh outlines a fluid compartment, not its microscopic lining.

articles.title: Myelin and rapid conduction
articles.summary: Insulating axon segments changes how an electrical signal travels along a fiber.
paragraphs: Myelin reduces membrane capacitance along insulated axon segments. Depolarization spreads between gaps called nodes, where voltage-gated channels regenerate the action potential. This node-to-node renewal is called saltatory conduction.

Oligodendrocytes form myelin in the central nervous system. White matter is rich in myelinated axons, but its surface mesh cannot show which individual axons are myelinated or how quickly they conduct.
articles.scope: This explanation describes a mechanism. The atlas has no electrical simulation, individual fibers, myelin measurements, or measured conduction speeds.

articles.title: How synapses pass a signal
articles.summary: Chemical transmission links presynaptic release to receptors on another cell.
paragraphs: At a typical chemical synapse, terminal depolarization opens calcium channels. Calcium entry promotes vesicle fusion and transmitter release. Transmitter acts on receptors across the synaptic cleft, changing the receiving cell’s electrical or biochemical state.

Excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic responses influence whether a neuron fires. Their effects depend on receptors, ion gradients, timing, and the other inputs arriving at that cell. A connection between regions does not specify all these mechanisms.
articles.scope: Synapses are not resolved in these meshes. Region connections are educational associations, not a measured synaptic wiring diagram or a simulation of thought.

articles.title: What counts as a brain cell type?
articles.summary: Shape, physiology, gene expression, and location reveal different aspects of cellular identity.
paragraphs: Siletti and colleagues profiled more than three million nuclei from adult human brain tissue. Their 2023 study reported 461 clusters and 3,313 subclusters, organized largely along developmental divisions. Those numbers describe a particular transcriptomic classification, not a final universal count of cell types.

RNA-based grouping helps distinguish populations that a large anatomical label combines. Sampling, analysis, species, age, and cell state matter when comparing taxonomies. The Allen Institute provides the human atlas data and its hierarchy for further exploration.
articles.scope: This reference links to human research; it does not import those cells into the 3D atlas. Cell classes are not assigned to individual mesh vertices, and mouse data must not be presented as measured human anatomy.

articles.title: What an atlas boundary means
articles.summary: A parcel is a region defined by a particular labeling method, with a particular resolution.
paragraphs: FreeSurfer’s Desikan–Killiany atlas divides the cortical surface using gyral anatomy and a learned labeling procedure. Its parcels are not equivalent to Brodmann’s cellular areas or to a functional map measured during a task.

Cerebra displays 68 cortical parcels plus 36 other segmented parts. A finer model adds geometric faces from a higher-resolution source surface. It does not add new internal structures, prove a functional boundary, or describe every individual’s anatomy.
articles.scope: Surface anatomy, cellular organization, and task activation are distinct measurements. The MRI templates, task maps, and surface model here come from separate sources; their spatial correspondence is not established by opening them in the same site.

articles.title: Common names and functional areas
articles.summary: Heschl’s gyrus, Broca’s area, and V1 do not all name the same kind of anatomical object.
paragraphs: A named gyrus describes a fold. A cytoarchitectonic area describes cellular organization. A functional area is characterized through physiological or behavioral evidence. Their borders need not coincide.

Structure search recognizes common names and shows the corresponding available parcels. Broca searches lead to the classical left inferior frontal landmarks; these parcels do not delineate an entire language system. Search notes explain each mapping and link its source.
articles.scope: Search aliases are navigation aids. They never create missing geometry or assert that a full parcel has one exclusive function.

explorations.note: Follow four anatomical stops in a distributed language system, with limits on classical localization.
